get_sample_densities#

class imbal.regression.get_sample_densities(labels, bandwidth, distribution=None, interpolation_method=None, interpolation_samples=None, atol=0, padding_factor=0.01, return_interpolation_samples=False)#

Bases:

This function exists as a means of extracting densities from a scitkit-learn KernelDensity object. As a part of this function, some approaches to improve time efficiency for KDE sampling have been included, which can cost at the cost of a small error in the desnity values sampled.

Kernel density estimatinon is defined as:

\[\hat{f}_h(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_h(x-x_i)\]

By definition, to compute the KDE of a single point, we require a summation of the density kernel centered at each known data point. Therefore, computing the KDE for a single label is an \(O(n)\) operation, and computing the KDE for each label is an \(O(n^2)\) operation. This means retreiving the densities for a large dataset will take a long time. To combat this, get_densities implements some approximation methods to reduce compute time.

The first of these approximation methods is allowing some absolute tolerance for the error of each KDE value (See: atol). This method is motivated by the fact that points that are far from one another contribute very little to each of their respective KDEs. By ignoring points far away from each point in the KDE calculation, we can achieve a faster KDE calculation while ensuring a maximum possible error.

For one dimensional data, we use a custom implementation that tends to yeilds results faster, which is implemented as follows:

  • We define \(\delta\) such that \(K(\delta) = \text{atol}\), where \(K\) is the Gaussian kernel. Or in other words, \(\delta\) is equal to the distance from the center of the Gaussian kernel which will produce a density value of atol (Concretely, \(\delta = K^{-1}(\text{atol})\)). Points beyond this distance \(\delta\) will produce a density less than atol.

  • We sort the data, then iterate through the list of data points. From the current point, \(p\), we find all points \(x \in [p - \delta, p + \delta]\)

  • For each point, we can determine a localized KDE estimate using only the points that fall within the delta range, that normalize the local KDE to the same scale as the full KDE.

The result of this method is an apporixmation of the full KDE, such that each approximated point has an error no greater than \(\text{atol}/n\), therefore the total error is no more than atol.

By working with the points in ascending order, the delta bounds for each point can be found in \(O(1)\) amortized time. We use this method as opposed to a binary search to find the bounds for each point, which would be an \(O(log(n))\) operation per point.

For multidimensional data, we leverage scikit-learn’s built-in atol for KDEs, which utilizes a KDTree to find its tolerance bounds. This way, the gains in computational performance can still be utilized for one dimensional data, without sacrificing loss of generality.

The second approximation method is an interpolation method. This method works by sampling evenly spaced points across the span of the provided dataset from the KDE, then using one of scipy’s RegularGridInterpolator interpolation methods to extrapolate the density values for the dataset. This method tends to be faster than using an absolute tolerance, at the cost of sometimes yielding less accurate results (with no guarentee of some maximum error).

Parameters:

  • labels – A NumPy array of labels, arranged as a column vector

  • bandwidth – The bandwidth that should be used to generate the KDE used for densit sampling

  • distribution – Optional, default None. A list of labels used to generate the KDE distribution. If set to None, the provided labels will be used to generate the distribution.

  • interpolation_method – Optional, default None. When not set as None, will be passed to a scipy RegularGridInterpolator as the method that should be used to interpolate between sampled points.

  • interpolation_samples – Optional, default None. The number of points to be sampled from the density distribution for interpolation. When set to None, this value is computed as labels.shape[0] / 10. If KDE was generated using imbal.regression.fit_kde, steps_per_bin*bin_count tends to be a good value for distribution_samples. This parameter is ignored when interpolation_method is set to None.

  • atol – Optional, default 1e-4. The maximum absolute error for each sample in the KDE.

  • return_interpolation_samples – Optional, default False If set to true, returns a tuple containing the list of x and y coordinates used to generate the optimized KDE. Mainly used for visualization.

  • padding_factor – Optional, default 0.01. Used to add a small padding to the data range used for binning for the histogram. See imbal.regression.fit_kde.

Returns:

A NumPy array of densities, arranged as a column vector

Examples

>>> labels = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 5])
>>> kde_bandwidth = imbal.regression.fit_kde(labels, bin_count=3)
>>> densities = imbal.regression.get_densities(labels, kde_bandwidth)

>>> print(densities)
[[1.0930867], [1.0930867], [1.0930867], [1.0930867], [1.0930867],
 [1.0930867], [0.5465676], [0.5465676], [0.5465676], [0.1821784]]

>>> # Local Approximation Example
>>> labels = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 5])
>>> kde_bandwidth = imbal.regression.fit_kde(labels, bin_count=3)
>>> local_approx_densities = imbal.regression.get_densities(
>>>     labels,
>>>     kde_bandwidth,
>>>     atol=1e-3
>>> )

>>> # For this example dataset, small errors are found in some densities
>>> print(local_approx_densities)
[[1.0930705], [1.0930705], [1.0930705], [1.0930705], [1.0930705],
 [1.0930705], [0.5465353], [0.5465353], [0.5465353], [0.1821784]]

>>> # Linear Interpolation Example
>>> labels = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 5])
>>> kde_bandwidth = imbal.regression.fit_kde(labels, bin_count=3)
>>> linear_interpolation_densities = imbal.regression.get_densities(
>>>     labels,
>>>     kde_bandwidth,
>>>     interpolation_method='linear',
>>>     interpolation_samples=5
>>> )

>>> # For this example dataset, small errors are found in all densities
>>> print(linear_interpolation_densities)
[[1.0392918], [1.0392918], [1.0392918], [1.0392918], [1.0392918],
 [1.0392918], [0.5255651], [0.5255651], [0.5255651], [0.1687906]]

Comparison of Methods in One Dimension#

The interpolations and absolute tolerance estimation methods exist for the generate_sample_weights, which can decrease the amount of computation time required to compute density values, at the cost of a small amount of error in these values. Below is a comparison of these estimation techniques with the regular full KDE computation across three different datasets.

Datasets#

For these comparisons, we have made use of three datasets, shown below. These datasets capture several scenarios for imbalanced data.

Argument for Improved 1D Case#

For data in one-dimension, we have manually implemented local approximation with absolute tolerance in a way that bypasses the scikit-learn KernelDensity object, avoiding some of the overhead it introduces to work in a general n-dimensional case. Our implementation results in significant time improvements across all datasets, as shown below. All tests in the table shown below were performed with an atol value of 1e-4, with no interpolation.
